newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo government vows comrehensive reforms.
newsitem.headline: Yugo government vows comrehensive reforms.

text.p: The Yugoslav government will insist on comprehensive reforms based on an open market economy harmonised with European Union (EU) economies, a senior government official said on Monday.
"There will be no partial steps, no cosmetic changes, but a complete programme of comprehensive reforms," new Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic told reporters.

Djunic was speaking at his first news conference since coming to office two weeks ago charged with a new porfolio including reforms, economic development and cooperation with international organisations.

The reforms will not be a single act or decision but an ongoing process that starts immediately, with the long-term goal of creating and maintaining a transparent institutional framework for a market economy compatible with the EU, he said.

"I am not setting out a programme of reforms today. That would be too pretentious after such a short time in office. I am only setting out a programme of work on reforms -- the rules and other basic postulates we will work on," Djunic said.
He said the government will continue to support the National Bank of Yugoslavia's independence and will not tap the central bank for its budget needs.

Yugoslavia will also pursue liberalisation and adjustment of its foreign trade regime to requirements of the World Trade Organisation and the EU, But results should not be expected overnight, he said.

"We will not fall into a trap of completely lifting protection and leaving the economy, exhausted by four years of sanctions, to the mercy of competition for which it is not and cannot be fully prepared. But we will not protect our economy at all costs either," Djunic said.
Yugoslav foreign trade has already been liberalised to a large extent, with only 13 percent of imports and eight percent of exports subject to quotas.
The main task in fiscal policy is to introduce a value added tax system, which the government hopes to become effective January 1, 1998.

Djunic said the military budget will be reduced to the level appropriate to GDP, while taking care not to jeopardise the country's security. Around 74 percent of the federal budget is currently set aside for the Yugoslav army.
The Yugoslav government will extend maximum support to ownership transformation and privatisation of the economy.
These are key instruments for structural adjustment and restructuring of firms as well as for the partial settlement of the problem of internal and external debts, Djunic said.
He said the government will insist on development of market institutions, above all the financial and labour markets.
One of the conditions for boosting the financial market is reform and rehabilitation of the banking sector.
"We are seriously counting on technical assistance from outside, from the EU through the Phare and Know-how programmes, and the United States through the USAID programme," Djunic said.
The aim of the reform programme is to set off an avalanche of private and individual initiatives to begin creating GDP, which is a precondition for a better life, he said.
Djunic said the work of the government would be more open to the public eye.
"One of my goals is precisely to change the government's image both at home and abroad and in that context we will insist on the government's work being completely public."
